name: Fatima Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Fatima. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Happy to. I'm Fatima, I'm 27, and I look after the orchard side of a mixed farm in the valley. It's mostly apples and pears, about forty hectares of trees, with sheep grazing between the rows in winter and a bit of hay on the flat fields.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: In winter it's pruning, every tree by hand with loppers, and my wrists know about it by February. In spring I'm up at four some nights checking the frost alarm, because one cold night at blossom time can take half the crop. September and October are the big months: I run a crew of about thirty pickers, sort out the bins, the ladders, the rotas, and argue with the packhouse about bruising. I love the trees, honestly. I don't love being the one who tells a picker from abroad that their pay is short because the fruit came in small.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Yusuf, who drives buses in town. We rent a flat above the bakery on Station Street. Money is tight, maybe three weeks of savings if we're lucky, and there are only two other orchards within an hour's drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. We call this one AI Plateau.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's the boring one, but boring isn't bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was oversold, and I'd be a bit smug about it, because the neighbours at Penrose Orchards tried a picking robot last autumn and it bruised every third pear. I'd say the tools are useful for small things, like translating the safety sheet for the pickers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad, but I'd know the hard stuff stays hard. Pickers still can't find housing, the price for apples still doesn't cover the cost of growing them, and nobody's fixing that with an app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the chat app for translations and frost forecasts, nothing more. I'd keep pushing the boss to sign up with the fair work scheme for seasonal workers, because that's the fight that matters in that picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit disappointed for the pickers, because a robot that did the night-time frost checks would have been nice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the frost checks. What's that like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At four in the morning, standing in the wet grass with a torch, looking at a thermometer. If AI could just do that part and leave me the trees, I'd sign up tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes at home in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, really. Same flat, same bakery smell, same worries about rent. We'd maybe start saving for a deposit, slowly.

S0.say: I'd say it was oversold, because the picking robot next door bruised every third pear. The tools help with small jobs, like translating the safety sheet for pickers.
S0.think: I'd be glad, but the hard problems stay hard. Pickers still can't find housing, and the apple price still doesn't cover the cost of growing them.
S0.do: Keeps using a chat app for translations and frost forecasts and nothing more. Keeps pressing her boss to join a fair work scheme for seasonal pickers.
S0.feel: Calm, with a little disappointment that nothing takes over the four o'clock frost checks.
S0.quote: If AI could just do that part and leave me the trees, I'd sign up tomorrow.
S0.fieldNote: Fatima is not against the technology; she wants it for the worst parts of the job, like night frost checks. Her worries in the calm picture are about pickers' housing and fruit prices. She already uses AI tools occasionally and practically, mostly to translate for the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. We call this one Steady Disruption.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I can actually picture. It's half happening already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to make sure the pickers aren't the ones who pay for it. I'd share stuff about seasonal workers' rights and say any farm getting public money for robots should have to retrain the people they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the picking crew shrinks first and my job changes rather than disappears. Somebody still has to decide which trees to prune and when to spray, and somebody has to watch the robots, and I'd want that to be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until Penrose or someone else gets a picking robot that actually works, then I'd ask the boss to send me on the supplier's training. I'd start using the orchard app for spray records properly, not just now and then. And I'd talk to the pickers early, the ones who come back every year, so they're not surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more for others than me. I'd feel a bit guilty learning the machine that replaces my crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there one picker you'd worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta. She's come back for seven seasons, she's the fastest picker we have, and she sends the money home to her mother. I'd want to help her find something, maybe as a robot supervisor too if they'd train her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd campaign for pickers but also learn the robot. Does that sit easily with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I think. I'd still argue for the pickers in public, and I'd still learn the robots myself. If I don't, someone from the city will come and do it for more money.

S1.say: I'd say the pickers mustn't be the ones who pay for it. Any farm getting public money for robots should have to retrain the people it replaces.
S1.think: I think the picking crew shrinks first and my own job changes rather than disappears. Somebody still decides on pruning and spraying and watches the robots, and I want that to be me.
S1.do: Waits until a neighbouring orchard proves a picking robot works, then asks for the supplier's training. Starts using the orchard app for spray records properly and warns returning pickers early.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mostly on her crew's behalf, with some guilt about learning the machine that replaces them.
S1.quote: If I don't, someone from the city will come and do it for more money.
S1.fieldNote: She holds two positions at once and is open about it: campaigning for pickers and learning the robots herself. Her steady style shows in waiting for a neighbour to prove a machine first. She thinks of a specific picker, Marta, before thinking about herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. We call this one AGI by 2028.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028? That's two pruning seasons. I'm not sure I believe it, but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has to be shared or it'll tear everything apart. I'd be signing every petition for a basic income, and saying the robot companies should pay into it, not just the farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm finished in this job, and so is the whole crew. With only two years, nobody's going to wait for proof, the price of fruit will drop the moment one big grower goes fully robotic, and our boss will have to follow or sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back hard, straight away, no holidays, the car goes and I'd bike. I'd sign up for any short course I could get on robot maintenance, even online, even though I'm not sure it'll matter. And I'd lean on Yusuf's job, if buses still need drivers by then, which they might not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Sort of sick in the stomach, like when the frost alarm goes off at blossom time and you know you're already too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change at home first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop talking about a house deposit. We'd probably move in with my sister for a while to save rent, which neither of us wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hold responsible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government, for not planning. And the big tech companies. Not the boss, he'd be just as stuck, and not the pickers, they'd be worse off than anyone.

S2.say: I'd say this has to be shared or it will tear everything apart. I'd sign every basic income petition and say the robot companies should pay into it.
S2.think: I think I'm finished in this job, along with the whole crew. With two years nobody waits for proof, the fruit price drops, and the boss has to follow or sell.
S2.do: Cuts spending at once, sells the car and cycles, and drops any holiday. Signs up for a short online robot maintenance course, and she and Yusuf may move in with her sister to save rent.
S2.feel: Scared and sick, like hearing the frost alarm at blossom time and knowing it's too late.
S2.quote: Sort of sick in the stomach, like when the frost alarm goes off at blossom time and you know you're already too late.
S2.fieldNote: The short warning time breaks her usual habit of waiting for proof, because she says there would be no time for proof. She still retrains, but with little hope it will count. Her household safety net is her partner's job and her sister's spare room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. We call this one AGI by 2031.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's at least enough time to see the robots arrive in the next orchard first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to get the rules right, and I'd mean it. I'd try to get the growers' group and the pickers' groups in one room, which would be a first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is my sweet spot. It's long enough to watch Penrose go first, see what works, and get trained before our boss buys anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd do an evening course in farm robotics at the college, the one that runs Tuesday nights. I'd put away a little each month, even forty or fifty, and I'd volunteer to run any robot trial on our farm. If the boss won't do a trial, I'd go and help at Penrose on my days off just to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. It's like knowing the frost is coming in three days instead of three hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the robots arrive and the boss decides he doesn't need you either?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd still have learned something useful and I'd look further away. I'd hate to leave the valley, but with five years I could plan it rather than run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your day look different in the first two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first couple of years, yes, about the same. I'd still prune, still run the crew, just with the course on top and one ear always open.

S3.say: I'd say we have five years to get the rules right. I'd try to get the growers' group and the pickers' groups into one room for the first time.
S3.think: Five years feels like my sweet spot. I could watch the next orchard go first, see what works, and get trained before our boss buys anything.
S3.do: Starts a Tuesday evening farm robotics course at the college in year one and saves forty or fifty a month. Volunteers to run any robot trial, or helps the neighbouring orchard on days off to learn.
S3.feel: Anxious but workable, like knowing the frost is three days off rather than three hours.
S3.quote: It's like knowing the frost is coming in three days instead of three hours.
S3.fieldNote: Five years suits her steady style best: time for someone else to prove the machines, and time for her to train. She is willing to leave the valley if needed but wants to plan it rather than run. She again tries to bring growers and workers together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. We call this one AGI by 2036.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That's a whole career change, if I wanted one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got no excuse this time. I'd want the growers to set up a shared robot fleet through a cooperative, owned by the farms and the workers together, so the money stays in the valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years is enough for me to end up running robots in the orchard instead of a crew. I'm not sure I'd love it as much as pruning by hand, but I'd still be among the trees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take it slowly: learn the orchard app properly this year, do the robotics course in two or three years once the kit is proven, and save what I can. I'd start talking up the cooperative idea at the growers' meetings now, because those things take years to get going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a small sad feeling about the pruning. I'd miss the loppers, strangely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the longer warning change any plans at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. We'd probably try for a baby sooner rather than later, while I'm still sure I've got work. Yusuf thinks that's backwards, but I'd rather have the baby while the job is solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who still worries you, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta and the others, again. Ten years is enough to retrain if someone pays for it, but most of them won't have that chance unless we push for it.

S4.say: I'd say there's no excuse this time. Growers and workers should own a shared robot fleet through a cooperative, so the money stays in the valley.
S4.think: Ten years is enough for me to end up running robots in the orchard instead of a crew. I might not love it as much as pruning, but I'd still be among the trees.
S4.do: Learns the orchard app properly this year and plans the robotics course in two or three years once the kit is proven. Starts pushing a growers' robot cooperative now and brings forward plans for a baby.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with a quiet sadness about losing hand pruning.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years she becomes a planner and an organiser, pitching a cooperative that both growers and workers would own. Her one family change is to have a baby sooner while work feels solid, which her partner questions. Her concern for the seasonal pickers runs through every picture.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because nobody gets time to prove anything and the pickers would be dropped overnight. What would help is retraining that's paid for, and a basic income if the jobs really go, funded by the companies that make the robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the pickers' side properly. Most of the people who'll lose out on farms like ours aren't even in your survey, because they're here for eight weeks a year.

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Thank you. I'd like to read what comes out of this, if I can.

headlineQuote: If AI could just do that part and leave me the trees, I'd sign up tomorrow.
portrait: Fatima is a 27-year-old orchard supervisor on a mixed farm built around apples and pears, living with her bus-driver partner Yusuf in a rented flat with about three weeks of savings. She uses AI tools now and then, mostly to translate for her seasonal picking crew, and she wants machines for the worst parts of the job, not the trees. Across the scenarios she waits for neighbours to prove new kit, but the two-year picture forces her to act without proof and leaves her alarmed. Five and ten years suit her steady nature: she plans evening training, saves small amounts and pushes for a growers' and workers' cooperative. Her concern for the pickers, especially a long-time worker called Marta, never leaves her.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI scenario, because there would be no time to prove anything and the pickers would be dropped overnight.
whatWouldHelp: Retraining that is paid for, and a basic income funded by the companies that make the robots if the jobs really go.
